idiom_name: std::vector<Entity*> cells[N * N] indexed by cell_y * N + cell_x
implementation_notes: Without a library dependency the pattern is hand-written: one std::vector<Entity*> per cell in a flat array indexed by cell_y * N + cell_x, with insert pushing and removal using std::erase or remove_if; the position-to-cell mapping is a division. std::vector's contiguous storage makes cell scans cache-friendly, and reallocation invalidates iterators, so per-object removal handles must be designed around that. The hand grid is the default when objects move every frame and queries are radius-shaped; the Boost.Geometry variant is preferable when queries are geometric over more static data.
pitfalls: Cells hold raw pointers and do not own entities: the partition must be updated on despawn or queries return dangling pointers.
push_back may reallocate a cell vector and invalidate stored iterators, so handle-based removal has to use indices or an erase-remove pass.
Removal from the middle of a cell vector is linear in the cell size; on hot paths swap-and-pop is usually better than std::erase.

variants.name: Boost.Geometry R-tree (bgi::rtree)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Geometry ships a real spatial index: bgi::rtree stores value types such as std::pair<box, Entity*> and supports insert, remove and query with spatial predicates (bgi::intersects for regions, bgi::nearest for k-nearest) as shown in the Quick Start. Choose it when queries are geometric and the indexed geometry changes less often than the query rate; for per-frame updates of many small movers the default hand grid is usually faster and simpler because R-tree insert/remove rebalance the tree.
pitfalls: Values are stored by copy: the indexed box must be kept in sync with the entity, and remove needs a value equal to the inserted one.
Nodes split by the chosen balancing algorithm; very large per-frame insertion rates degrade performance compared with a flat grid.
A query returns values in unspecified order and a broad box query can still return many candidates, so the exact predicate remains necessary.
